lessons.title: Lazy Loading & Viewport Tracking via IntersectionObserver
lessons.description: Detect when elements enter or leave the viewport without expensive scroll event listeners.

sections.heading: What is IntersectionObserver?
paragraphs: IntersectionObserver asynchronously observes changes in the intersection of an element with its ancestor or the viewport. It's the modern way to implement lazy loading and infinite scroll.
list: Replaces scroll event listeners for viewport detection
Runs off the main thread — no performance impact
Use for: lazy loading images, infinite scroll, ad viewability

codeExamples.heading: Lazy loading images
explanation: IntersectionObserver watches elements and fires when they enter the viewport.
rootMargin: 200px starts loading before the element is visible.
unobserve() stops watching after the image loads — cleanup.
This runs off the main thread — no scroll jank.

practice.task: Implement lazy loading for 10 images using IntersectionObserver. Show a placeholder until each image enters the viewport.
hints: Set data-src on images with a placeholder src.
Create an observer that loads data-src when intersecting.
Add rootMargin to preload images before they're visible.

keyTakeaways: IntersectionObserver detects when elements enter the viewport.
It's asynchronous and runs off the main thread — no performance impact.
Use rootMargin to preload content before it's visible.
Perfect for lazy loading, infinite scroll and ad viewability tracking.
lessons.challenge: Build an infinite scroll feed that loads more content when the user scrolls near the bottom.

lessons.title: Tracking Element Bounds via ResizeObserver
lessons.description: Detect when an element's size changes — useful for responsive layouts and dynamic content.

sections.heading: What is ResizeObserver?
list: Observes changes to an element's content rect or border box
Replaces window.resize for element-specific size tracking
Runs off the main thread — no performance impact
Use for: responsive components, chart resizing, layout adjustments

codeExamples.heading: ResizeObserver in action
explanation: ResizeObserver fires whenever the observed element's size changes.
contentRect gives you the element's dimensions.
It runs off the main thread — safe for frequent size changes.
Much more efficient than window.resize for element-specific tracking.

practice.task: Use ResizeObserver to track a div's dimensions and display them in real-time as the user resizes the browser.
hints: Display the dimensions in a fixed-position element.

keyTakeaways: ResizeObserver detects when an element's size changes.
It's more efficient than window.resize for element-specific tracking.
contentRect provides the element's current dimensions.
Perfect for responsive components and dynamic layout adjustments.
lessons.challenge: Build a responsive sidebar that uses ResizeObserver to adjust its content layout based on its current width.

lessons.title: Performance Metrics: Core Web Vitals (INP, LCP, CLS) & PerformanceObserver
lessons.description: Measure and monitor key performance metrics that affect user experience and SEO rankings.

sections.heading: Core Web Vitals
list: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) — how fast the main content loads
INP (Interaction to Next Paint) — responsiveness to user interactions
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) — visual stability during loading
These metrics directly impact Google search rankings

codeExamples.heading: Measuring Core Web Vitals
explanation: PerformanceObserver watches for performance events asynchronously.
LCP measures when the largest visible element finishes painting.
CLS measures layout shifts that happen without user input.
buffered: true includes events that already happened.

practice.task: Use PerformanceObserver to measure and log the LCP and CLS of your web page.
hints: Log the values: entry.startTime for LCP, entry.value for CLS.

keyTakeaways: Core Web Vitals measure real user experience: loading speed, responsiveness, visual stability.
LCP, INP and CLS directly impact SEO and user satisfaction.
Always measure before optimizing — know what to improve.
lessons.challenge: Build a performance dashboard that displays real-time Core Web Vitals using PerformanceObserver.

lessons.title: Scheduling Idle Tasks via requestIdleCallback
lessons.description: Run low-priority work during browser idle time — don't block the main thread.

sections.heading: What is requestIdleCallback?
list: Runs a callback when the browser is idle (no urgent work)
Provides a deadline object to manage time budget
Automatically paused when the tab is not visible
Use for: analytics, prefetching, non-urgent background work

codeExamples.heading: requestIdleCallback usage
explanation: deadline.timeRemaining() tells you how much idle time is left.
Process as many tasks as time allows, then yield.
If tasks remain, schedule another idle callback.
This ensures low-priority work never blocks rendering.

practice.task: Use requestIdleCallback to process a queue of 100 items without blocking the main thread. Process items only during idle time.
hints: If time runs out, schedule another callback.
Items should be processed gradually, not all at once.

keyTakeaways: requestIdleCallback runs work during browser idle time.
deadline.timeRemaining() tells you how much time you have.
Never block the main thread — yield when time runs out.
Perfect for analytics, prefetching and other non-urgent work.
lessons.challenge: Build a background data processor that handles 1000 items using requestIdleCallback without blocking the UI.
